stem: You are the obstetric registrar receiving a 31-year-old G3P2 at 32+1 weeks referred with confirmed spontaneous rupture of membranes at 30 minutes ago. Speculum examination confirms pooling of clear liquor with pH-positive testing and negative ferning-alternative tests unnecessary. There is no bleeding, no chorioamnionitis features, and no maternal fever. Cervix is closed on visual inspection. Foetal HR 145 with normal reactivity. Ultrasound shows AFI 6 cm, singleton cephalic, EFW 1810 g (50th centile). She has no penicillin allergy and no other medical problems. Her previous two pregnancies delivered at term uneventfully.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 84, blood pressure 118/72, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius, foetal HR 145
data_table.Examination: Sterile speculum shows clear liquor pooling, closed visual cervix, no bleeding, no offensive discharge
data_table.Investigations: White cells 9.4 x10^9/L (5.0-11.0), CRP 3 mg/L (<5), CTG reactive baseline 145 variability 10-25 bpm, AFI 6 cm, EFW 1810 g at 50th centile, GBS status unknown from this pregnancy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management plan?

options.text: Admit for expectant management to 37 weeks with betamethasone plus oral erythromycin 250 mg 6-hourly for 10 days
options.rationale: RANZCOG guidance for PPROM between 24+0 and 33+6 weeks without infection or foetal compromise is expectant management to prolong pregnancy, with corticosteroids (betamethasone 11.4 mg IM x2) for foetal lung maturity, erythromycin (avoid co-amoxiclav in this indication because of neonatal necrotising enterocolitis signal in ORACLE I) for 10 days to prolong latency, and intrapartum GBS prophylaxis given unknown GBS status. Aim for delivery by 37+0 weeks to balance prematurity and infection risk. (Source: RANZCOG PPROM)

options.text: Proceed to immediate category-1 caesarean section today for foetal safety given confirmed spontaneous rupture of membranes
options.rationale: Delivery is triggered by infection, foetal compromise, placental abruption, or reaching 37 weeks. In its absence, expectant management until 37 weeks improves neonatal outcomes because prematurity below 34 weeks poses more risk than the current infectious threat. (Source: RANZCOG PPROM)

options.text: Discharge home on oral azithromycin 1 g weekly with weekly outpatient obstetric ultrasound review until 37 weeks
options.rationale: Discharge home is not recommended for PPROM before 34 weeks because of the risk of rapid deterioration from chorioamnionitis, abruption or cord accident. Inpatient care with regular CTG and infection surveillance is preferred. (Source: RANZCOG PPROM)

options.text: Commence intravenous ampicillin plus gentamicin and induce labour with an oxytocin infusion titrated over 12 hours
options.rationale: Broad-spectrum IV antibiotics and induction are used when chorioamnionitis is diagnosed. In their absence at 32 weeks, expectant management is preferred to allow further foetal lung maturation. (Source: RANZCOG PPROM)

options.text: Give magnesium sulfate 4 g loading dose immediately and defer antenatal corticosteroids for 48 hours of observation
options.rationale: Magnesium sulfate is given for neuroprotection when delivery is anticipated within 24 hours and gestation is less than 30 to 32 weeks; at 32+1 with no evidence of imminent delivery it is not routinely given. Steroids should not be deferred; they are given at diagnosis of PPROM 24 to 34 weeks. (Source: RANZCOG PPROM)

explanation.summary: PPROM between 24+0 and 33+6 weeks without infection or foetal compromise is managed expectantly to prolong pregnancy with antenatal corticosteroids for lung maturity and prophylactic erythromycin for 10 days to reduce infection and delay delivery. Amoxicillin-clavulanate is avoided because of increased neonatal necrotising enterocolitis risk (ORACLE I). Intrapartum GBS prophylaxis is given empirically when GBS status is unknown at delivery. Delivery is planned by 37+0 weeks.
key_points: PPROM 24-33+6 weeks without infection: expectant management with steroids + 10 day erythromycin
Corticosteroids: betamethasone 11.4 mg IM two doses 24 h apart (or dexamethasone 6 mg IM x4 12 h apart)
Amoxicillin-clavulanate contraindicated in PPROM (NEC signal in ORACLE I)
Deliver by 37+0 to balance prematurity vs infection risk
explanation.pearls: Magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection is loaded 4 g IV over 20 minutes then 1 g/hour infusion when delivery is anticipated within 24 hours at <30-32 weeks gestation.

stem: You are the antenatal clinic obstetric registrar reviewing a 34-year-old G2P1 at 36+3 weeks. Her first pregnancy ended in emergency classical vertical caesarean section at 30 weeks for placenta praevia with catastrophic haemorrhage and preterm PROM. The operation note confirms a classical upper-segment incision was made because the lower segment was poorly formed and inaccessible. Her current pregnancy is a singleton cephalic and has been uncomplicated. She has read about VBAC on the internet and is asking whether she can have a trial of labour to avoid another caesarean. She has no other medical or surgical history and no allergies. She is well engaged in shared decision-making and asks for a clear recommendation.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 78, blood pressure 118/74, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius, foetal HR 140
data_table.Examination: Fundal height 36 cm, cephalic presentation, longitudinal lie, engaged head not deep, no abdominal tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Ultrasound confirms singleton cephalic, EFW 2860 g at 50th centile, anterior placenta well away from previous scar, AFI 12 cm; operative note from prior CS confirms classical vertical upper-segment incision

options.text: Support planned trial of labour after previous caesarean with continuous cardiotocography in the tertiary birthing suite
options.rationale: Trial of labour is contraindicated when the prior caesarean incision was classical (vertical upper-segment) because rupture risk approaches 10 to 12% versus <1% for low-transverse. RANZCOG advises against labour in this scenario. (Source: RANZCOG VBAC)

options.text: Recommend planned elective repeat caesarean section at 37+0 weeks after a shared-decision discussion of rupture risk
options.rationale: A prior classical (vertical upper-segment) caesarean is an absolute contraindication to trial of labour because uterine rupture rate is 10 to 12% versus under 1% for a single low-transverse incision. RANZCOG recommends elective repeat caesarean at 37+0 to 38+0 weeks to reduce the risk of labour onset while balancing neonatal maturation. Shared decision-making is documented but the recommendation should be specific. (Source: RANZCOG VBAC)

options.text: Perform elective repeat caesarean section today at 36+3 weeks under regional anaesthesia in a tertiary theatre
options.rationale: Elective delivery before 37+0 without a specific indication increases neonatal respiratory morbidity. Timing of elective repeat caesarean after classical incision is typically 37+0 to 38+0 weeks. (Source: RANZCOG VBAC)

options.text: Manage expectantly with cervical scoring at 40 weeks and induction using dinoprostone if the cervix is unfavourable
options.rationale: Prostaglandin cervical ripening is contraindicated after prior classical caesarean because of markedly increased rupture risk. Expectant management to 40 weeks is inappropriate given rising labour probability. (Source: RANZCOG VBAC)

options.text: Offer an external cephalic version with oxytocin augmentation because the placenta is implanted anteriorly today
options.rationale: The baby is already cephalic, and oxytocin augmentation in a prior classical caesarean is contraindicated. External cephalic version has no role for a cephalic-presenting foetus. (Source: RANZCOG VBAC)

explanation.summary: Trial of labour after caesarean is contraindicated when the prior incision was classical (vertical upper-segment), T-incision, or inverted-T because of a substantially higher uterine rupture risk (10 to 12% vs <1% for a single low-transverse scar). RANZCOG recommends elective repeat caesarean at 37+0 to 38+0 weeks. Prostaglandin cervical ripening and oxytocin augmentation are contraindicated in prior classical caesarean pregnancies planned for delivery.
key_points: Prior classical (vertical upper-segment) CS = absolute contraindication to trial of labour
Rupture risk classical incision 10-12% vs low-transverse <1%
Elective repeat CS at 37+0 to 38+0 weeks after prior classical incision
Prostaglandin cervical ripening contraindicated after any prior CS scar (RANZCOG)
explanation.pearls: Other absolute contraindications to VBAC: prior uterine rupture, T-shaped or inverted-T scar, transverse lie or breech in labour, placenta praevia or accreta.

sources.label: RCOG Green-top 45 Birth After Caesarean Birth

stem: You are the on-call obstetric registrar reviewing a 33-year-old G3P2 at 36+4 weeks referred by ambulance with sudden onset of severe abdominal pain and moderate vaginal bleeding 45 minutes ago. She has smoked 20 cigarettes per day throughout pregnancy and had gestational hypertension diagnosed at 34 weeks with labetalol 200 mg BD. She is haemodynamically stable. On examination the uterus is tender and firm with palpable contractions every 3 minutes, she has passed approximately 400 mL of dark red blood, cervix is 3 cm on speculum and admits one finger, and the placenta was previously confirmed fundal. CTG shows a baseline of 140, variability 10 to 25 bpm, moderate variable decelerations recovering to baseline, with no late decelerations.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 96, blood pressure 138/86, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius, foetal HR baseline 140
data_table.Examination: Tender firm uterus with contractions every 3 minutes lasting 60 s, cervix 3 cm on speculum, active moderate PV bleeding estimated at 400 mL
data_table.Investigations: haemoglobin 108 g/L (115-165), platelets 168 x10^9/L (150-400), fibrinogen 3.2 g/L (2-4), INR 1.1, group and hold sent, CTG reactive baseline 140 with recovering moderate variable decelerations

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Give a further loading dose of magnesium sulfate 4 g intravenously for eclampsia prophylaxis and monitor CTG for 4 hours
options.rationale: The primary problem here is placental abruption at term with active bleeding, contractions and non-reassuring foetal patterns tending to deteriorate. Delaying delivery for magnesium prophylaxis exposes both mother and foetus to further catastrophic haemorrhage. If gestational hypertension had progressed to severe pre-eclampsia with imminent eclampsia signs, magnesium would be part of management but does not delay delivery in an active abruption. (Source: RANZCOG APH)

options.text: Give subcutaneous terbutaline 250 microgram as tocolysis to permit transfer to a tertiary obstetric centre now
options.rationale: Tocolysis is contraindicated in active abruption because it may worsen bleeding and delay definitive delivery. It is not part of the management pathway. (Source: RANZCOG APH)

options.text: Prepare for immediate category-1 caesarean, secure two large-bore intravenous cannulae, and cross-match four units
options.rationale: Suspected placental abruption at 36+4 weeks with active bleeding, tender firm uterus, contractions and foetal compromise warrants urgent delivery. At term or near-term with foetal or maternal compromise, this is by caesarean unless vaginal delivery is genuinely imminent. Two large-bore IV cannulae, cross-match, coagulation studies, MTP awareness (Hb 108, likely underestimates true loss, fibrinogen still normal but consumption risk is high) and neonatal team activation are the concurrent steps. (Source: RANZCOG APH)

options.text: Insert an indwelling urinary catheter, give intravenous tranexamic acid 1 g, and reassess CTG in 30 minutes
options.rationale: TXA and urinary catheterisation are useful adjuncts, but a 30-minute wait for reassessment is unsafe in the presence of active abruption with foetal compromise and heavy loss. Delivery should not be delayed. (Source: RANZCOG APH)

options.text: Commence an oxytocin infusion to augment labour and aim for vaginal delivery with continuous cardiotocography
options.rationale: Oxytocin augmentation in a bleeding, abrupting uterus at 3 cm cervical dilation without foetal head deep in the pelvis is dangerous and takes hours to achieve delivery. Category 1 caesarean is the safest route. (Source: RANZCOG APH)

explanation.summary: Suspected placental abruption near term with active bleeding, uterine tenderness and any foetal compromise mandates urgent delivery, usually by category 1 caesarean unless vaginal delivery is imminent. Two large-bore IVs, cross-match, coagulation studies, and readiness to activate the massive transfusion protocol are simultaneous. Fibrinogen is a sensitive marker of consumption and DIC risk. Neonatal team must be present.
key_points: Placental abruption at term with maternal or foetal compromise = urgent delivery, usually category 1 CS
Two large-bore IVs, cross-match 4 units, group + coagulation profile including fibrinogen
Fibrinogen <2 g/L in obstetric haemorrhage is an early trigger for cryoprecipitate
Tocolysis contraindicated in active abruption; oxytocin augmentation contraindicated when delivery is not imminent
explanation.pearls: Peripartum fibrinogen normally rises to 4-6 g/L; a fibrinogen <2 g/L in obstetric haemorrhage predicts progression to massive haemorrhage and is an early cryoprecipitate trigger.

stem: You are the psychiatry registrar called by the postnatal ward at 02:00. A 32-year-old primipara is 9 days postnatal after a normal vaginal delivery. Over the last 48 hours she has been increasingly agitated, sleeping less than 2 hours per night, speaking pressured and rapidly about needing to protect the baby from spiritual harm, and today insisted the baby is possessed and requires cleansing rituals. She has personal history of bipolar I disorder untreated in pregnancy following her decision to stop lithium 3 years ago when planning conception. Her mother had a psychiatric admission after her own second child was born. On assessment tonight she is disorientated to date, has fluctuating attention, and told the midwife earlier that she saw shadows moving around the baby's cot. Baby is currently with her partner in the ward.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 112, blood pressure 128/78, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 37.1 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count within normal limits, TSH 1.2 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), electrolytes and calcium within normal limits, urinalysis clear, no illicit substance use, CT head deferred pending medical review
data_table.History: 9 days postpartum, prior bipolar I stopped lithium 3 years ago, maternal aunt puerperal admission, agitation with delusional beliefs about baby, hallucinations reported, sleep <2 h nightly for 48 h

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management step?

options.text: Discharge overnight with the partner as informal supervision and outpatient perinatal team follow-up in 48 hours
options.rationale: Postpartum psychosis is a psychiatric emergency with elevated risk of maternal suicide and infanticide. Discharge home is unsafe even with informal partner supervision. (Source: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health)

options.text: Prescribe oral zopiclone 7.5 mg nightly to normalise sleep and review the ward assessment during daytime rounds
options.rationale: A sedative-hypnotic alone will not address the psychotic illness, offers no antipsychotic effect, and leaves the mother and baby at ongoing risk. Sleep is important but is a consequence not the driver of the emergency. (Source: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health)

options.text: Remove the baby from the ward tonight and commence sertraline 50 mg for postpartum depression with psychotic features
options.rationale: This is postpartum psychosis, not postpartum depression, and starting an SSRI alone is inadequate. Bipolar-spectrum postpartum psychosis is typically managed with lithium and an atypical antipsychotic, not SSRI monotherapy. Baby separation is a decision made in collaboration with the mother-baby unit and child protection colleagues, not unilaterally at the outset. (Source: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health)

options.text: Admit to a mother-baby psychiatric unit under mental health legislation and start olanzapine with perinatal plan
options.rationale: Postpartum psychosis (delusions about the baby, disorientation, hallucinations, sleep disturbance) with prior bipolar I disorder and a family history of puerperal psychosis carries very high risk of maternal suicide and infanticide. Admission to a mother-baby psychiatric unit under mental health legislation with continuous observation, commencement of an atypical antipsychotic acutely, and specialist perinatal assessment to reinstate lithium (weighing feeding decisions) is the RANZCP-endorsed pathway. Baby remains with mother in supervised MBU setting where clinically safe. (Source: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health)

options.text: Give intramuscular haloperidol 10 mg and physical restraint pending transfer to a general adult psychiatric unit
options.rationale: Non-emergency use of physical restraint and high-dose typical antipsychotic monotherapy is not the first step; oral atypical antipsychotic is preferred where the patient can accept oral medication. Transfer to a general adult unit rather than a mother-baby unit fragments care and separates baby from mother without clear necessity. (Source: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health)

explanation.summary: Postpartum psychosis is a psychiatric emergency, typically onset within the first 2 weeks, with delusions (often about the baby), sleep disturbance, agitation and disorientation. Bipolar I history and family history of puerperal psychosis substantially raise risk. Management requires urgent admission to a mother-baby psychiatric unit where possible, mental health legislation involvement, atypical antipsychotic and specialist perinatal review for lithium reinstatement.
key_points: Postpartum psychosis: onset <2 weeks postpartum with delusions, hallucinations, disorientation, sleep loss
Prior bipolar I and family history of puerperal psychosis carry >30% recurrence risk
MBU admission preferred; MHA framework used when insight impaired
Lithium is highly effective but excreted in breast milk; specialist decision on feeding
explanation.pearls: Puerperal psychosis with bipolar I background has a 30-50% recurrence risk in subsequent pregnancies; antenatal lithium prophylaxis after obstetric-psychiatric consultation reduces recurrence.

sources.label: COPE Perinatal Mental Health National Guideline

stem: You are the mental health registrar reviewing a 20-year-old male university student in a community psychiatric emergency clinic. Over the past 6 weeks he has developed persecutory delusions about being tracked by a coordinated group, auditory hallucinations of two voices commenting on his behaviour, and social withdrawal. Onset was gradual over 4 weeks; the last 2 weeks his function has collapsed. He commenced daily high-potency cannabis (~1.5 g/day of a THC-dominant product) 12 months ago and stopped completely 3 weeks ago on family insistence. There is no other substance use, no alcohol above two standard drinks per week, no synthetic cannabinoid use, no prescribed medications, no head injury, no seizure history. There is a family history of schizophrenia in a maternal uncle. Mental state examination confirms first-rank symptoms with preserved orientation.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 78, blood pressure 122/74, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count within normal limits, TSH 1.6 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), electrolytes and calcium within normal limits, LFTs normal, urine drug screen positive for cannabinoids (from prior use, up to 30 days), negative for methamphetamine and cocaine, CT head normal
data_table.History: 6 weeks psychotic symptoms, cannabis daily 12 months then stopped 3 weeks ago, no other substances, family history schizophrenia (maternal uncle), function collapsed over 2 weeks

lead_in: How would you formulate this presentation and what is the most appropriate initial pharmacological plan?

options.text: Diagnose cannabis-induced psychotic disorder likely to resolve within 24 hours and observe without any antipsychotic
options.rationale: Cannabis-induced psychotic disorder typically resolves within 1 month of abstinence in true cases. This patient has been abstinent for 3 weeks with persistent worsening symptoms and 2 weeks of collapsed function, suggesting a primary psychotic disorder or cannabis has unmasked a primary process. Observation without treatment is unsafe. (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia)

options.text: Commence lorazepam 1 mg twice daily as required and defer antipsychotic while awaiting spontaneous resolution over weeks
options.rationale: Benzodiazepine monotherapy has no antipsychotic activity and does not address the underlying illness. Delaying antipsychotic prolongs untreated psychosis, which is associated with worse long-term functional outcome. (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia)

options.text: Commence sertraline 50 mg daily as first-line therapy for likely major depression with psychotic features
options.rationale: The presentation is a primary psychotic disorder (persecutory delusions, auditory hallucinations, 6 weeks duration, collapsed function) rather than depression with psychotic features. Mood symptoms are secondary and an SSRI alone is inadequate. (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia)

options.text: Commence quetiapine 100 mg titrated to 400 mg over 4 weeks as first-line therapy for likely bipolar depression
options.rationale: There is no history of mood episodes, no elevated or depressed mood, and no relevant family history of bipolar disorder here. Diagnosing bipolar disorder without any mood evidence is unsupported. (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia)

options.text: Commence risperidone titrated to 2 to 4 mg, refer to early psychosis intervention, and provide cannabis relapse plan
options.rationale: Persistent psychotic symptoms 3 weeks after cannabis cessation with 6 weeks total duration, collapsed function and a family history of schizophrenia meet criteria for a schizophrenia-spectrum first episode psychosis. Cannabis is best formulated as a precipitating rather than sole cause. RANZCP and Australian EPPIC guidance is early antipsychotic (low-dose atypical such as risperidone or olanzapine), early intervention service referral, psychoeducation about cannabis as a relapse and severity driver, and safety planning. (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia)

explanation.summary: Cannabis-induced psychotic disorder typically resolves within 4 weeks of abstinence. Persistent psychotic symptoms 3 weeks after cessation with collapsed function and family history of schizophrenia are more consistent with a schizophrenia-spectrum first episode of psychosis, with cannabis as a precipitating factor. Australian EPPIC guidance is early antipsychotic (low dose), early psychosis intervention team referral, psychoeducation and safety planning.
key_points: Cannabis-induced psychotic disorder should resolve within ~4 weeks of abstinence
Persistent symptoms beyond that = re-diagnose as primary psychotic disorder (cannabis precipitant)
First-episode psychosis pharmacotherapy: low-dose atypical (risperidone 1-4 mg, olanzapine 5-10 mg)
Cannabis use increases lifetime schizophrenia risk 2-4 fold; high-potency THC increases it further
explanation.pearls: Cannabis-related psychotic conversion to schizophrenia occurs in ~34% of cannabis-induced psychosis cases at 8-year follow-up (Danish register data 2018).

subtopic_detail: Autism spectrum disorder in adult women
stem: You are the general practice registrar in an adult clinic. A 28-year-old professional woman presents with 12 months of severe fatigue and burnout following a workplace restructure. She reports lifelong difficulty with sustained group social interaction, exhaustion after work social events, intense special interests (medieval history, and prior periods of hyper-focused folklore research), sensory sensitivities to fluorescent light and clothing labels, and a longstanding sense of masking to fit in socially. She has previously been diagnosed with anxiety and depression at ages 16 and 22 with only partial response to sertraline and CBT. She has close but limited friendships with women who share her special interests. Her general practitioner is considering a formal neurodevelopmental assessment. She is not autistic-identifying at this time. She has no psychotic features, no substance use, and no mood elevation.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 74, blood pressure 118/74, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count within normal limits, ferritin 62 mcg/L (30-300), vitamin D 68 nmol/L (>50), TSH 2.1 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), electrolytes and glucose within normal limits, PHQ-9 12 (mild-moderate), GAD-7 14 (moderate), AUDIT 3, PDSS-SR 6
data_table.History: 12 months burnout, lifelong social difficulty, intense special interests, sensory sensitivities, masking; prior anxiety and depression diagnoses partially responsive to sertraline and CBT; no psychosis, no substances, no mood elevation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in your assessment plan?

options.text: Refer for structured autism assessment with ADOS-2 and ADI-R and continue psychological therapy for anxiety in parallel
options.rationale: The presentation (lifelong social exhaustion, intense special interests, sensory sensitivities, masking, and partial response to standard anxiety and depression care with recurrent burnout) is characteristic of previously-undiagnosed autism spectrum disorder in an adult woman. Australian adult ASD guidance (RANZCP and the Australian National Guideline for Assessment) supports structured assessment with clinicians experienced in the female phenotype, using ADOS-2 and ADI-R alongside a developmental history from a childhood informant. Concurrent management of comorbid anxiety and burnout continues in parallel. (Source: Australian ASD Diagnostic Guideline)

options.text: Reassure her this is generalised anxiety disorder and increase sertraline to the maximum dose of 200 mg daily
options.rationale: The clinical picture is far broader than an anxiety disorder alone. Increasing sertraline to maximum without addressing the underlying neurodevelopmental profile misses the primary diagnostic question and repeats prior partial-response cycles. (Source: RANZCP ADHD/ASD adult resources)

options.text: Perform brief AQ-10 screening and, if score under 6, discharge from any further adult neurodevelopmental workup
options.rationale: The AQ-10 is a screen with moderate sensitivity; a low score should not exclude ASD when the clinical picture is strongly suggestive, and it is known to underdetect the female phenotype. Structured assessment remains warranted. (Source: Australian ASD Diagnostic Guideline)

options.text: Commence a trial of methylphenidate 10 mg daily for suspected adult attention deficit hyperactivity disorder empirically
options.rationale: Empirically starting stimulant medication without a diagnostic assessment for ADHD is not appropriate. In addition, the presentation here fits ASD better than adult ADHD, though the two can co-occur; formal assessment first is essential. (Source: RANZCP ADHD/ASD adult resources)

options.text: Refer for inpatient adult psychiatric admission today for stabilisation of burnout and multi-system fatigue symptoms
options.rationale: There is no risk to self or others, no severe functional collapse requiring inpatient care, and no psychotic or manic features. Outpatient assessment and support is appropriate. (Source: RANZCP ADHD/ASD adult resources)

explanation.summary: Undiagnosed adult female ASD often presents in the general practice or adult psychiatry clinic as recurrent burnout, partial response to standard depression and anxiety care, and lifelong social masking with sensory sensitivities and intense circumscribed interests. Structured assessment with clinicians experienced in the female phenotype, using ADOS-2 and ADI-R with childhood informant history, is the standard in Australia. Concurrent management of comorbid anxiety and depression continues.
key_points: Female ASD presentation: masking, exhaustion after socialising, intense special interests, sensory sensitivities, partial response to anxiety/depression care
AQ-10 sensitivity is modest, especially in the female phenotype; do not use as a rule-out
ADOS-2 + ADI-R + childhood informant history is standard adult diagnostic assessment
Comorbid anxiety, depression, ADHD common; manage in parallel
explanation.pearls: Adult women may not receive an ASD diagnosis until their 30s-40s despite lifelong features, because clinician training and screening tools were largely designed on male childhood samples.

subtopic_detail: Sepsis hour-1 bundle and vasopressor initiation
stem: You are the medical registrar in an Australian emergency department. A 68-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes and moderate CKD (baseline creatinine 130 micromol/L) is brought in with rigors, dysuria, right-flank pain and confusion. She is quickly recognised as having urosepsis. Within 30 minutes she has received IV gentamicin 5 mg/kg and IV amoxicillin-clavulanate. She has received 30 mL/kg of balanced crystalloid over 90 minutes. Her repeat lactate 60 minutes after starting fluids has risen from 4.2 to 5.1 mmol/L. She remains hypotensive with mean arterial pressure of 58 mmHg despite the completed bolus. Blood cultures were drawn before antibiotics.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 118, blood pressure 82/44 (MAP 58), respiratory rate 26, SpO2 96% on 4 L nasal prongs, temperature 39.1 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: white cells 22.4 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), CRP 316 mg/L (<5), lactate 5.1 mmol/L (was 4.2), sodium 132 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 4.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), creatinine 240 micromol/L (baseline 130), venous pH 7.28 (7.35-7.45), bicarbonate 16 mmol/L, urinalysis heavy nitrites and blood
data_table.History: T2DM, CKD baseline creatinine 130, urosepsis on antibiotics for 45 minutes, 30 mL/kg balanced crystalloid completed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Give a further 30 mL/kg crystalloid bolus over 60 minutes and reassess lactate and blood pressure in one hour
options.rationale: The Surviving Sepsis Campaign hour-1 bundle recommends initial crystalloid 30 mL/kg. Repeat 30 mL/kg fluid boluses beyond the initial resuscitation risk pulmonary oedema without addressing MAP. When MAP <65 after adequate initial fluid, vasopressor initiation is preferred rather than repeated boluses. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)

options.text: Commence peripheral noradrenaline infusion via a large-bore antecubital vein while central access is being established
options.rationale: The SSC and ANZICS guidance is to start noradrenaline early when MAP remains under 65 despite adequate initial crystalloid (30 mL/kg). Peripheral noradrenaline infusion through a large-bore proximal vein (antecubital or larger) is now supported for up to 24 hours or bridging to central access, and delays from waiting for central access are associated with worse outcomes. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)

options.text: Give intravenous hydrocortisone 200 mg loading dose before starting vasopressor therapy for septic shock
options.rationale: Hydrocortisone is added when noradrenaline requirement exceeds 0.25 microgram/kg/min or when shock is refractory. It is not routinely given before vasopressor initiation. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)

options.text: Escalate to intravenous meropenem 1 g plus vancomycin loading dose 25 mg/kg for likely resistant urosepsis coverage
options.rationale: For community-acquired urosepsis, gentamicin plus amoxicillin-clavulanate provides adequate empiric coverage per Australian Therapeutic Guidelines. Escalation to broader spectrum with MRSA cover is not indicated in this scenario and does not address the immediate perfusion failure. (Source: eTG Antibiotic Urosepsis)

options.text: Delay commencing vasopressor therapy until the mean arterial pressure falls below 55 mmHg despite ongoing fluids
options.rationale: Delaying vasopressor risks prolonged tissue hypoperfusion. MAP target is 65 mmHg or above after initial fluid resuscitation; failure to meet this triggers noradrenaline. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)

explanation.summary: Rising lactate 60 minutes after adequate initial crystalloid resuscitation with persistent MAP under 65 mmHg indicates fluid-refractory septic shock. The Surviving Sepsis Campaign hour-1 bundle then calls for noradrenaline titrated to MAP at least 65 mmHg. Peripheral noradrenaline through a large-bore proximal vein is acceptable as a bridge to central access. Hydrocortisone is added if vasopressor requirement is high (typically noradrenaline >=0.25 microgram/kg/min).
key_points: Hour-1 sepsis bundle: measure lactate, blood cultures before antibiotics, broad-spectrum IV antibiotics, 30 mL/kg crystalloid, vasopressor if MAP <65 after fluid
Noradrenaline is first-line vasopressor; peripheral use safe as bridge to central access
MAP target 65 mmHg or above (higher in chronic hypertension may be considered)
Add hydrocortisone 200 mg/day if noradrenaline >=0.25 mcg/kg/min or refractory
explanation.pearls: The 30 mL/kg initial fluid bolus is calculated on actual body weight in most Australian ED protocols; use ideal body weight in class III obesity to avoid over-resuscitation.

subtopic_detail: First demyelinating event and McDonald criteria
stem: You are the neurology registrar reviewing a 28-year-old woman referred by her general practitioner. Over the last 10 days she has developed progressive vision loss in her right eye with pain on eye movement. Ten months ago she had a 3-week episode of numbness across the right hemibody that resolved fully and she attributed it to stress and did not seek medical review at the time. She has no other medical history and takes no medications. On examination today her right visual acuity is 6/24 with a right relative afferent pupillary defect and a subtle red desaturation on the right; left eye 6/6. Neurological examination is otherwise normal. Fundoscopy shows a mildly swollen right optic disc.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 76, blood pressure 122/78, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count within normal limits, TSH within normal limits, HIV and syphilis serology negative, ANA negative, vitamin B12 380 pmol/L (>200), MRI brain and spine shows one enhancing right optic nerve lesion plus 4 non-enhancing periventricular T2 lesions plus 1 spinal cord T2 lesion at C4 plus 1 juxtacortical T2 lesion, no infratentorial lesion, CSF oligoclonal bands positive (not present in serum), aquaporin-4 antibody negative, MOG-IgG negative
data_table.History: 10 months ago transient right hemibody numbness for 3 weeks, now right optic neuritis, no other medical history, no medications

lead_in: What is the most appropriate diagnostic conclusion and next step?

options.text: Clinically isolated syndrome with insufficient evidence for a multiple sclerosis diagnosis; repeat magnetic resonance imaging in 3 months
options.rationale: The prior transient hemibody numbness followed by optic neuritis today represents two clinical attacks in different sites, and MRI demonstrates lesions in more than one typical MS location. Dissemination in space and time is met, so a diagnosis of multiple sclerosis can be made now rather than deferring to CIS. (Source: RACP Multiple Sclerosis Diagnosis)

options.text: Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder based on optic and spinal cord involvement; commence rituximab this admission
options.rationale: Aquaporin-4 antibody negative, MOG-IgG negative, the MRI pattern (multiple typical MS locations without long spinal cord lesions >=3 vertebral segments), and CSF pattern all favour MS over NMOSD. Rituximab is not first-line without a NMOSD diagnosis. (Source: RACP Multiple Sclerosis Diagnosis)

options.text: Relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis meeting 2017 McDonald criteria; give IV methylprednisolone and refer for DMT
options.rationale: This patient has two clinical attacks (prior hemibody sensory episode plus current optic neuritis) with objective clinical evidence for the current attack (relative afferent pupillary defect, reduced acuity, red desaturation, swollen disc). MRI shows lesions in at least two of the four typical MS locations (periventricular, juxtacortical, cortical, infratentorial, spinal cord), satisfying dissemination in space. CSF-specific oligoclonal bands provide additional support and can substitute for dissemination in time under 2017 criteria. Acute optic neuritis is treated with IV methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 3 to 5 days; DMT selection is a neurologist-led decision. (Source: RACP Multiple Sclerosis Diagnosis)

options.text: Myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein-antibody-associated disease; commence high-dose oral prednisone taper only today
options.rationale: MOG-IgG is negative in this patient and the MRI does not show characteristic MOG features (long spinal cord or bilateral optic nerve lesions). Steroid monotherapy alone is not the appropriate long-term approach for MS. (Source: RACP Multiple Sclerosis Diagnosis)

options.text: Anti-N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor encephalitis; refer for ovarian teratoma workup and plasmapheresis this admission
options.rationale: Anti-NMDA encephalitis presents with subacute psychiatric symptoms, seizures, movement disorders and autonomic instability rather than optic neuritis with typical MS MRI findings and MS-pattern oligoclonal bands. (Source: RACP Multiple Sclerosis Diagnosis)

explanation.summary: Two clinical attacks with objective evidence for at least one and MRI dissemination in space (lesions in at least two typical MS locations) satisfy the 2017 McDonald criteria for relapsing-remitting MS at first neurology contact. CSF-specific oligoclonal bands can substitute for dissemination in time. Acute optic neuritis is treated with IV methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 3 to 5 days. Disease-modifying therapy selection is neurologist-led and depends on disease activity, comorbidities and pregnancy plans.
key_points: 2017 McDonald criteria: DIS = lesion in >=2 of 4 typical MS regions (periventricular, juxtacortical/cortical, infratentorial, spinal); DIT = simultaneous asymptomatic + symptomatic lesion or new lesion on follow-up MRI or CSF-specific OCBs
Acute optic neuritis: IV methylprednisolone 1 g/day for 3-5 days; hastens recovery but does not change final visual outcome (ONTT)
DMT choice ranges from teriflunomide/glatiramer/interferon to natalizumab, ocrelizumab, ofatumumab, cladribine
Negative AQP4-IgG and MOG-IgG plus positive OCBs supports MS over NMOSD/MOGAD
explanation.pearls: The Optic Neuritis Treatment Trial showed IV methylprednisolone accelerates visual recovery in first 2 weeks but does not affect final visual acuity at 12 months; oral prednisone alone showed higher relapse rate.

stem: You are the medical registrar in the emergency department resuscitation cubicle. A 62-year-old man presented 20 minutes ago with sudden onset dyspnoea and syncope 40 minutes after arriving from an interstate flight. He is now clammy, breathless and confused. Point-of-care ultrasound shows a dilated right ventricle with poor contractility. Bedside troponin is 380 ng/L (upper reference 30) and NT-proBNP is 3400 pg/mL. He weighs 92 kg. His IV access is patent. He has no active bleeding, no recent surgery, no stroke, no known intracranial pathology, no bleeding disorder, no anticoagulation, no allergy. His wife confirms no head injury and no gastrointestinal bleeding in the last month.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 128, blood pressure 76/42, respiratory rate 34, SpO2 88% on 15 L non-rebreather, temperature 36.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: troponin 380 ng/L (<30), NT-proBNP 3400 pg/mL (<450), lactate 3.8 mmol/L (<2), venous pH 7.30 (7.35-7.45), full blood count within normal limits, INR 1.1, creatinine 96 micromol/L (60-110), point-of-care ultrasound dilated hypokinetic right ventricle with septal flattening; CT pulmonary angiogram unavailable in the next 10 minutes
data_table.History: Long-haul flight, sudden dyspnoea and syncope, no bleeding, no surgery, no stroke, no intracranial pathology, no anticoagulation, no allergy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Commence unfractionated heparin infusion at 80 units per kilogram bolus and await computed tomography pulmonary angiography
options.rationale: In high-risk (haemodynamically unstable) suspected pulmonary embolism where imaging is not immediately available, empiric systemic thrombolysis is recommended after weighing bleeding risk; delaying to await confirmatory imaging risks death from ongoing right ventricular failure. (Source: ANZ Society for Vascular Medicine PE guidance)

options.text: Commence intravenous adrenaline infusion, intubate for airway control, and defer thrombolysis until CT head done
options.rationale: There are no clinical features of intracranial haemorrhage. Delaying thrombolysis for a routine CT head in the absence of neurological signs adds mortality. Intubation may further compromise haemodynamics in massive PE due to loss of intrinsic sympathetic drive and worsening venous return. (Source: ANZ Society for Vascular Medicine PE guidance)

options.text: Give an intravenous 20 mL/kg fluid bolus and add dobutamine infusion for right ventricular support without thrombolysis
options.rationale: Aggressive volume loading in RV failure worsens septal displacement and reduces LV filling further. Small volume challenges (250-500 mL) may be considered, but ionotropic support alone without addressing the clot is insufficient for high-risk PE. (Source: ANZ Society for Vascular Medicine PE guidance)

options.text: Administer systemic alteplase 100 mg intravenously over 2 hours with concurrent unfractionated heparin per protocol
options.rationale: This is high-risk (massive) pulmonary embolism (sustained hypotension with RV dysfunction and biomarker elevation). ESC and ANZ guidance recommend systemic thrombolysis with alteplase 100 mg IV over 2 hours (or 0.6 mg/kg over 15 minutes up to 50 mg in cardiac arrest) with no absolute contraindications present. Anticoagulation is continued around the infusion per local protocol. Noradrenaline is preferred as vasoactive support in RV failure. (Source: ESC PE Guidelines 2019)

options.text: Refer for emergency surgical pulmonary embolectomy without giving any medical thrombolysis first this admission
options.rationale: Surgical embolectomy is reserved for patients with absolute contraindications to thrombolysis or failed thrombolysis, and access is limited to specialised centres. It is not first-line when systemic thrombolysis is available and safe. (Source: ESC PE Guidelines 2019)

explanation.summary: High-risk pulmonary embolism (persistent hypotension with right ventricular dysfunction and biomarker elevation) has 30-day mortality of 20 to 30% without reperfusion. Systemic thrombolysis with alteplase 100 mg over 2 hours (or 0.6 mg/kg over 15 minutes in cardiac arrest) is the ESC first-line therapy when no absolute contraindications are present. Noradrenaline supports RV perfusion; dobutamine adds inotropy if inotropic failure predominates. Catheter-directed thrombolysis or surgical embolectomy are alternatives in centres where systemic lysis fails or is contraindicated.
key_points: High-risk PE (persistent hypotension + RV dysfunction + elevated biomarkers) requires immediate reperfusion
Systemic alteplase 100 mg IV over 2 hours is first-line if no absolute contraindication
Absolute contraindications: haemorrhagic stroke ever, ischaemic stroke <6 mo, active bleeding, intracranial neoplasm, recent major surgery or head trauma <3 weeks
Noradrenaline preferred vasopressor in acute RV failure; avoid aggressive fluid loading
explanation.pearls: Alteplase reduced-dose regimen (0.6 mg/kg IV over 15 minutes, max 50 mg) is used during cardiac arrest with suspected PE, per ANZCOR guidance.

stem: You are the fellow in a maternal-foetal medicine clinic at a tertiary referral hospital. A 36-year-old G4P3 at 30+2 weeks has been referred with placenta praevia on 20-week ultrasound. She has had 3 prior lower-segment caesarean sections and a dilation and curettage after a first-trimester miscarriage 2 years ago. Repeat greyscale and colour Doppler ultrasound at 30 weeks shows an anterior placenta covering the internal os with 2 large lacunae, a hypoechoic myometrial interface with the bladder wall of less than 1 mm in places, and increased subplacental vascularity. Bladder wall bulging is present. She has no antepartum bleeding today. She is asymptomatic. MRI has been booked for tomorrow morning.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 76, blood pressure 118/72, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius, foetal HR 145
data_table.Examination: Fundal height 30 cm, no abdominal tenderness, no palpable bladder, no active PV bleeding, cephalic presentation on Leopold's manoeuvre
data_table.Investigations: Ultrasound anterior praevia covering os, 2 large lacunae, myometrium-bladder interface <1 mm, bladder-wall bulging, increased subplacental vascularity; MRI booked for tomorrow morning; haemoglobin 118 g/L (115-165), platelets 220 x10^9/L, group and antibody screen O positive

lead_in: What is the most appropriate delivery planning strategy?

options.text: Plan vaginal delivery at 39 weeks with continuous cardiotocography and postpartum haemorrhage readiness in the birth suite
options.rationale: Placenta praevia with strong ultrasound features of placenta accreta spectrum absolutely contraindicates a vaginal delivery attempt because of catastrophic haemorrhage risk. Delivery is by planned caesarean at a tertiary centre. (Source: RANZCOG Placenta accreta spectrum)

options.text: Plan lower-segment caesarean at 39+0 weeks by the on-call obstetrician after in utero transfer to a regional hospital
options.rationale: Placenta accreta spectrum requires multidisciplinary tertiary-centre management. Regional facilities without interventional radiology, cell salvage, immediate blood products and colorectal or urological backup are the wrong setting, and delivery timing at 39 weeks is too late. (Source: RANZCOG Placenta accreta spectrum)

options.text: Plan classical caesarean at 34+0 weeks with attempted piecemeal manual placental removal to avoid hysterectomy today
options.rationale: Attempted forced placental removal in placenta accreta spectrum precipitates massive haemorrhage. The standard approach when accreta is confirmed is caesarean-hysterectomy with the placenta left in situ, or occasionally a conservative leave-in-situ approach in highly selected cases. (Source: RANZCOG Placenta accreta spectrum)

options.text: Plan elective preterm caesarean at 32+0 weeks with vertical skin incision without steroids or magnesium neuroprotection
options.rationale: Delivery at 32 weeks is earlier than recommended when the mother is stable and asymptomatic; RANZCOG recommends 34+0 to 35+6 weeks for suspected placenta accreta spectrum unless bleeding, contractions, or foetal compromise force earlier delivery. Antenatal corticosteroids and magnesium neuroprotection should also be given for planned preterm delivery. (Source: RANZCOG Placenta accreta spectrum)

options.text: Plan elective caesarean-hysterectomy at 34+0 to 35+6 weeks in a tertiary centre with multidisciplinary team present
options.rationale: Suspected placenta accreta spectrum with strong ultrasound features and prior caesarean history should be delivered by planned caesarean at 34+0 to 35+6 weeks in a tertiary centre with a dedicated multidisciplinary team. Standard care includes antenatal corticosteroids for lung maturity, planned caesarean-hysterectomy with the placenta left in situ (preferred to piecemeal removal), interventional radiology for possible internal iliac balloon occlusion, urology on standby for possible bladder involvement, cell salvage, and pre-optimisation of iron stores. RANZCOG endorses this pathway. (Source: RANZCOG Placenta accreta spectrum)

explanation.summary: Placenta accreta spectrum with strong antenatal ultrasound features (lacunae, myometrial thinning, bladder wall bulging, hypervascularity) in the setting of prior caesarean plus praevia is managed by planned caesarean at 34+0 to 35+6 weeks in a tertiary centre. Multidisciplinary team includes maternal-foetal medicine, interventional radiology, urology, senior anaesthesia, neonatology and blood bank. Standard operative approach is caesarean-hysterectomy with placenta left in situ rather than attempted removal.
key_points: Placenta accreta spectrum: deliver 34+0 to 35+6 weeks by planned caesarean at tertiary centre
Multidisciplinary team: MFM, IR, urology, senior anaesthesia, senior neonatology, blood bank
Standard operation: caesarean-hysterectomy with placenta left in situ (do not attempt removal)
Pre-optimise iron; antenatal corticosteroids for preterm delivery; consider cell salvage
explanation.pearls: Sensitivity of ultrasound plus colour Doppler for placenta accreta approaches 90% in high-volume centres; MRI adds most value for suspected posterior placentation or when depth of invasion (percreta) is unclear.

stem: You are the maternal-foetal medicine registrar reviewing a 26-year-old primigravida at 20+3 weeks with a monochorionic diamniotic twin pregnancy. She was booked at 12 weeks with chorionicity confirmed. Serial ultrasound today shows twin 1 with deepest vertical pocket (DVP) 2 cm, twin 2 with DVP 12 cm, twin 1 bladder not visualised over the 60-minute scan, twin 2 EFW 20% larger than twin 1, both twins with normal umbilical artery Doppler and normal middle cerebral artery Doppler, and normal ductus venosus Doppler in both twins. There is no evidence of foetal hydrops. She has no contractions, no bleeding, cervix is 34 mm on transvaginal ultrasound. She lives 3 hours drive from the nearest fetal therapy centre.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 78, blood pressure 118/74, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius, twin 1 foetal HR 148, twin 2 foetal HR 152
data_table.Investigations: Ultrasound monochorionic diamniotic twins, twin 1 DVP 2 cm with bladder not visualised for 60 minutes (donor), twin 2 DVP 12 cm (recipient), EFW discordance 20%, umbilical artery Doppler normal both twins, MCA Doppler normal both twins, ductus venosus Doppler normal both twins, no hydrops, cervix 34 mm
data_table.History: Primigravida, monochorionic diamniotic twins confirmed at 12 weeks, 3-hour drive from fetal therapy centre, no contractions or bleeding

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer urgently today to a national fetal therapy centre for consideration of fetoscopic laser photocoagulation
options.rationale: This is Quintero Stage II twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome: oligohydramnios in donor (DVP 2 cm at 20 weeks; less than 2 cm is required for stage I; combined with non-visualised bladder over 60 minutes moves to Stage II), polyhydramnios in recipient (DVP >8 cm before 20 weeks or >10 cm after 20 weeks). Stage II or higher TTTS between 16 and 26 weeks is managed with fetoscopic laser ablation of placental anastomoses, which improves at least one twin survival from 33% (amnioreduction alone) to 76% (Eurofetus and Solomon trials). Australian fetal therapy is centralised at select tertiary centres and urgent referral today is essential to allow assessment and intervention within the treatable window. (Source: RANZCOG Monochorionic Twin Pregnancy)

options.text: Perform therapeutic amnioreduction at the local hospital and continue serial ultrasound assessments every 2 weeks
options.rationale: Serial amnioreduction has substantially inferior outcomes to fetoscopic laser for Stage II or higher TTTS between 16 and 26 weeks (Eurofetus trial: laser survival benefit sustained at 6 months). It is retained as a temporising measure only when laser is not available or the woman is beyond the treatable gestational window. (Source: RANZCOG Monochorionic Twin Pregnancy)

options.text: Recommend expectant management with weekly ultrasound and no intervention until Doppler indices become abnormal
options.rationale: Once Quintero Stage II is reached, intervention improves outcomes substantially. Waiting for Doppler abnormalities allows progression to Stage III or IV where perinatal outcomes are markedly worse. (Source: RANZCOG Monochorionic Twin Pregnancy)

options.text: Discuss selective feticide of the donor twin now as the preferred first-line intervention at this gestation
options.rationale: Selective feticide is reserved for cases with impending demise of one twin or where laser is contraindicated or unsuccessful. It is not first-line when fetoscopic laser remains a treatment option. (Source: RANZCOG Monochorionic Twin Pregnancy)

options.text: Plan urgent delivery this week by caesarean section given the current Quintero staging and gestational age
options.rationale: Delivery at 20 weeks is not survivable. Delivery for TTTS is planned around 34 to 37 weeks after successful in utero treatment, unless earlier for obstetric or foetal reasons. (Source: RANZCOG Monochorionic Twin Pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Quintero staging for twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome: Stage I (donor DVP <2 cm with recipient DVP >8 cm before 20 weeks or >10 cm after 20 weeks), Stage II (bladder not visualised in donor for at least 60 minutes), Stage III (abnormal Doppler in either twin), Stage IV (hydrops in either twin), Stage V (in utero demise of one or both twins). Stage II or higher between 16 and 26 weeks is treated with fetoscopic laser photocoagulation of placental anastomoses at a fetal therapy centre. Eurofetus RCT showed superiority over amnioreduction.
key_points: Quintero Stage II TTTS: oligohydramnios donor, polyhydramnios recipient, donor bladder not visualised in 60 min
Fetoscopic laser ablation for Stage II or higher between 16-26 weeks is standard of care
Eurofetus RCT: laser at least one twin survival 76% vs amnioreduction 51%; better neurological outcomes at 6 months
Amnioreduction reserved for beyond treatable window or centre inaccessibility
explanation.pearls: Australian fetal therapy is centralised (Sydney, Melbourne, Brisbane) and referral is national; treating within Quintero Stage II or III before hydrops onset offers best neurodevelopmental outcomes.

stem: You are the consultation-liaison psychiatry registrar called to see a 22-year-old woman on the medical ward. She was admitted 3 days ago via emergency after 2 weeks of subacute onset of behavioural change (odd laughter, agitation), paranoid delusions, and orofacial dyskinesias. During today's ward round she had a 90 second focal aware seizure with right facial twitching and afterwards was mute for 20 minutes. Vital signs earlier showed transient tachycardia to 138 and blood pressure fluctuation between 92/58 and 168/98 within 30 minutes. The bedside neurological examination is inconsistent. She has no prior psychiatric or seizure history. She does not smoke, drink alcohol or use illicit substances. Screening MRI brain has been reported as normal.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 118 with fluctuation, blood pressure fluctuating 92/58 to 168/98, respiratory rate 20, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 37.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: full blood count within normal limits, urea 5.1 mmol/L (2.5-7.5), creatinine 68 micromol/L (60-110), C-reactive protein 12 mg/L (<5), TSH within normal limits, HIV and syphilis serology negative, urine drug screen negative, MRI brain normal, EEG shows generalised slowing with extreme delta brush pattern intermittently, CSF pleocytosis 42 white cells/microL with lymphocyte predominance and elevated CSF protein 0.68 g/L (<0.45), CSF glucose within normal limits, oligoclonal bands positive
data_table.History: 2 weeks subacute behavioural change, dyskinesias, focal seizure today, autonomic instability, no substances, no prior psychiatric or neurological history

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence olanzapine 10 mg orally daily for suspected first-episode psychosis and defer further neurological workup
options.rationale: The pentad of subacute behavioural change, orofacial dyskinesias, focal seizure, autonomic instability, and characteristic EEG (extreme delta brush) with CSF pleocytosis is highly suggestive of anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis. Antipsychotic monotherapy without further workup will not treat the underlying process and antipsychotics may worsen catatonic and NMS-like features. (Source: RANZCP Autoimmune Encephalitis)

options.text: Send CSF and serum for anti-NMDA antibody, image pelvis for teratoma, and start empirical first-line immunotherapy
options.rationale: The clinical picture is classic anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis: female patient in her early 20s with subacute psychiatric symptoms, dyskinesias, seizures, autonomic instability, and characteristic EEG (extreme delta brush) with CSF lymphocytic pleocytosis and elevated protein. In young women, ovarian teratoma is present in over 50% and its removal is part of definitive treatment. Australian and international neurology guidance is to send CSF and serum for anti-NMDA IgG, image for tumour, and commence first-line immunotherapy (steroids plus IVIG or plasma exchange) empirically pending antibody confirmation because early treatment improves outcomes. (Source: RANZCP Autoimmune Encephalitis)

options.text: Commence sertraline 50 mg daily for likely conversion disorder and refer to outpatient psychiatry follow-up
options.rationale: Conversion disorder is a diagnosis of exclusion and cannot account for CSF pleocytosis, an abnormal EEG with extreme delta brush, autonomic instability and focal seizure. Missing autoimmune encephalitis has serious consequences. (Source: RANZCP Autoimmune Encephalitis)

options.text: Load with sodium valproate 20 mg/kg intravenously and monitor for further seizures without further diagnostic workup
options.rationale: Sodium valproate is contraindicated in a 22-year-old woman of reproductive age without a proven epilepsy diagnosis and without pregnancy prevention counselling. It also does not address the underlying autoimmune process. (Source: RANZCP Autoimmune Encephalitis)

options.text: Refer for electroconvulsive therapy given the presence of catatonic features and prominent orofacial dyskinesias
options.rationale: ECT may have a role in refractory catatonia in autoimmune encephalitis but is not the initial step; immunotherapy plus tumour search is the priority. Using ECT without addressing the underlying autoimmune process is inappropriate. (Source: RANZCP Autoimmune Encephalitis)

explanation.summary: Anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis presents with a characteristic pentad of subacute behavioural change, dyskinesias, seizures, autonomic instability and dysphasic mutism, most commonly in young women. Extreme delta brush on EEG is highly specific and CSF typically shows lymphocytic pleocytosis with elevated protein. In women under 45, ovarian teratoma is present in more than half of cases and its removal is part of definitive treatment. First-line immunotherapy (methylprednisolone plus IVIG or plasma exchange) is started empirically pending antibody confirmation. Rituximab and cyclophosphamide are second-line for refractory disease.
key_points: Pentad: behavioural change, dyskinesias, seizures, autonomic instability, dysphasic mutism
EEG extreme delta brush is highly specific
CSF: lymphocytic pleocytosis + elevated protein + positive oligoclonal bands; anti-NMDA antibody in serum + CSF (CSF more sensitive)
Ovarian teratoma in >50% of women <45; removal is part of definitive treatment
explanation.pearls: Anti-NMDA CSF antibody sensitivity ~100% vs ~85% in serum; testing both increases yield. Rituximab is added when there is no response to first-line therapy within 2 weeks.

stem: You are the senior psychiatry registrar reviewing a 34-year-old man with schizophrenia. He has failed adequate trials (>=6 weeks at target dose) of risperidone 6 mg, olanzapine 20 mg and paliperidone 12 mg. Two years ago clozapine was commenced but ceased at week 3 for probable clozapine-induced myocarditis (troponin rise to 220 ng/L, CRP 82 mg/L, echocardiogram showed globally reduced LV function with EF 42%, no other cause identified). He was rehospitalised. Over the past 2 years he has been on aripiprazole 30 mg plus lurasidone 120 mg with persistent auditory hallucinations, negative symptoms and social withdrawal. Most recent echocardiogram (this week) shows LV EF 60% with no wall motion abnormality. He has been abstinent from all recreational substances for 12 months. Cardiology has been consulted.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 78, blood pressure 118/76, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count with neutrophils 4.8 x10^9/L (2.0-7.5), C-reactive protein 3 mg/L (<5), troponin 6 ng/L (<15), NT-proBNP 62 pg/mL (<125), echocardiogram LV EF 60% with no wall motion abnormality and no diastolic dysfunction, ECG sinus rhythm QTc 420 ms
data_table.History: Schizophrenia with failure of 3 adequate atypical trials, clozapine ceased for myocarditis 2 years ago, current medications aripiprazole + lurasidone with persistent positive and negative symptoms, cardiology reviewed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step for symptom control?

options.text: Refer for maintenance bilateral electroconvulsive therapy three times weekly indefinitely as ongoing symptom control
options.rationale: Maintenance ECT is used selectively when medication cannot achieve adequate response, but it does not replace an antipsychotic trial that could still deliver superior outcome. Clozapine remains the strongest evidence-based agent for treatment-resistant schizophrenia and should be re-considered before indefinite ECT is chosen. (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia Guidelines)

options.text: Add high-dose quetiapine 800 mg nightly to the current aripiprazole plus lurasidone regimen and continue indefinitely
options.rationale: Polypharmacy with three atypical antipsychotics has no evidence base, substantially increases metabolic, cardiac (QT prolongation) and anticholinergic burden, and does not achieve the response rate of a clozapine trial in treatment-resistant schizophrenia. (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia Guidelines)

options.text: Undertake supervised clozapine re-challenge with slower titration and structured cardiac surveillance with cardiology
options.rationale: Treatment-resistant schizophrenia (failure of 2 or more adequate trials at target dose) is the specific indication for clozapine. Prior clozapine-induced myocarditis is a relative not absolute contraindication; Australian case series describe successful re-challenge in about half of selected patients using slower titration and structured cardiac surveillance in collaboration with cardiology. Current cardiac status (normal EF, normal troponin, no ongoing cardiac abnormality) supports a considered re-challenge with informed consent. Clinical guidelines require weekly troponin and CRP for at least the first 4 weeks with prompt cessation on rise. (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia Guidelines)

options.text: Discontinue all antipsychotic medication and manage with high-dose lorazepam 4 mg four times daily for symptom control
options.rationale: Benzodiazepine monotherapy is not an evidence-based treatment for schizophrenia and increases risks of dependence, sedation and respiratory depression. It offers no antipsychotic activity. (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia Guidelines)

options.text: Add long-acting paliperidone 150 mg intramuscular injection monthly to the current oral aripiprazole and lurasidone
options.rationale: The patient has already failed adequate trials of paliperidone (12 mg oral, equivalent to LAI). Repeating an ineffective agent does not resolve treatment resistance and adds side-effect burden. Clozapine trial is the evidence-based next step. (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Treatment-resistant schizophrenia (failure of two adequate antipsychotic trials) is treated with clozapine. Prior clozapine-induced myocarditis is a relative rather than absolute contraindication; supervised re-challenge with slower titration and structured cardiac surveillance in collaboration with cardiology has been successful in approximately half of published Australian cases. Polypharmacy with additional atypical antipsychotics has no evidence base and increases metabolic and cardiac burden.
key_points: Treatment-resistant schizophrenia = failure of >=2 adequate trials of different antipsychotics at target dose
Clozapine is the definitive agent; re-challenge after prior myocarditis is possible in selected patients with cardiology co-management
Slower clozapine titration + weekly troponin and CRP for 4 weeks; stop and refer immediately on any rise
Baseline and follow-up echocardiogram; ECG at baseline, week 2, week 4
explanation.pearls: Clozapine-induced myocarditis usually occurs in the first 4 weeks; a slower titration (25 mg every 3-4 days initially) plus vigilant surveillance halves incidence of severe cases in Australian re-challenge protocols.

subtopic_detail: Neonatal seizure with normal blood glucose
stem: You are the neonatal registrar called to a term-born day 2 male infant on the postnatal ward. Birthweight 3410 g, Apgar 9 and 9 at 1 and 5 minutes, uncomplicated pregnancy and delivery, mother well and afebrile, no perinatal risk factors identified, breastfeeding established. The nurse describes a 90-second episode of tonic-clonic movement of the left arm with lip smacking, apnoea to SpO2 of 82%, and eye deviation to the left. Postictally he is drowsy but rousable. Bedside blood glucose is 3.4 mmol/L, capillary blood gas is normal, temperature is 36.9 degrees Celsius, no history of maternal opioid or SSRI exposure. His father reports that his own brother had recurrent neonatal seizures that resolved by 6 months without long-term epilepsy.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 148, respiratory rate 42, SpO2 98% on room air post-event, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius, capillary refill 2 seconds
data_table.Examination: Anterior fontanelle soft flat, tone normal, moro symmetric, no dysmorphic features, no skin lesions on Wood's lamp, cord well healed, no organomegaly, no bruises
data_table.Investigations: Bedside glucose 3.4 mmol/L (>2.6), capillary blood gas within normal limits, full blood count within normal limits, C-reactive protein 3 mg/L (<5), calcium ionised 1.20 mmol/L (1.10-1.30), magnesium 0.82 mmol/L (0.70-1.10), sodium 138 mmol/L (135-145)
data_table.History: Term uncomplicated pregnancy, no maternal opioid or SSRI exposure, family history of paternal uncle with self-resolving neonatal seizures

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence oral phenytoin 5 mg/kg every 12 hours and discharge to the postnatal ward on standard observations
options.rationale: Oral phenytoin absorption in neonates is erratic and phenytoin is not first-line for neonatal seizure. Discharge to routine observation misses the essential workup for infection and structural cause. (Source: RCH CPG Neonatal seizures)

options.text: Reassure the family this is likely jitteriness given the normal blood glucose and observe on the postnatal ward
options.rationale: This event is not consistent with benign neonatal jitteriness: jitteriness is stimulus-sensitive, stoppable with limb hold, and lacks eye deviation, apnoea and postictal drowsiness. The presentation is a focal clonic seizure requiring urgent workup. (Source: RCH CPG Neonatal seizures)

options.text: Give intramuscular vitamin K 1 mg and observe on the postnatal ward for further seizure activity before any workup
options.rationale: Vitamin K is important for haemostasis but does not treat or diagnose neonatal seizure. Deferring workup means missing time-critical causes such as meningitis or hypoglycaemia recurrence. (Source: RCH CPG Neonatal seizures)

options.text: Transfer to special care nursery for septic screen, empirical antibiotics plus acyclovir, EEG, MRI and metabolic panel
options.rationale: A term neonate with a focal clonic seizure of this description and a family history of self-limited familial neonatal epilepsy (KCNQ2 phenotype) requires broad emergency workup because early identification of infection (bacterial meningitis, HSV encephalitis), stroke, structural brain lesion, and inborn errors of metabolism (pyridoxine-dependent seizure, urea cycle defect) is time-critical. RCH and PSANZ neonatal seizure guidance mandate full septic screen with lumbar puncture, empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics plus acyclovir, EEG, cranial imaging and metabolic workup including a pyridoxine trial. First-line acute anticonvulsant is phenobarbitone 20 mg/kg IV. (Source: RCH CPG Neonatal seizures)

options.text: Perform a diagnostic lumbar puncture only and manage empirically as bacterial meningitis given the family history
options.rationale: A single positive family history is not diagnostic and the workup must be broader; anticonvulsant plans, imaging, metabolic testing and cover for HSV encephalitis must accompany the septic workup. Narrow investigation risks missing critical causes. (Source: RCH CPG Neonatal seizures)

explanation.summary: A term neonate with a focal seizure and normal blood glucose requires urgent transfer to a special care nursery for broad workup: full septic screen including lumbar puncture, empirical antibiotics plus acyclovir for HSV encephalitis, urgent EEG, cranial imaging (ultrasound then MRI), metabolic panel including plasma amino acids, ammonia, lactate, acylcarnitine profile and a pyridoxine trial. First-line anticonvulsant for recurrent seizure is phenobarbitone 20 mg/kg IV. Family history of self-limited familial neonatal epilepsy is a diagnosis of exclusion after infection, structural and metabolic causes are excluded.
key_points: Neonatal seizure with normal BSL: broad workup including septic screen with LP, empirical Abx + acyclovir, EEG, MRI, metabolic panel including pyridoxine trial
First-line acute anticonvulsant: phenobarbitone 20 mg/kg IV; second-line phenytoin 20 mg/kg IV
HSV encephalitis in neonate can present with focal seizure without skin lesions; empirical acyclovir is mandatory until PCR back
Self-limited familial neonatal epilepsy (KCNQ2) is a diagnosis of exclusion; suspicion warrants genetic panel
explanation.pearls: Pyridoxine-dependent seizure responds to 100 mg IV pyridoxine given during EEG-monitored administration; presence of seizure cessation is diagnostic and requires life-long supplementation.

subtopic_detail: Cardiogenic shock post-STEMI mechanical circulatory support
stem: You are the cardiology registrar in the coronary care unit. A 64-year-old man had a large anterior STEMI 6 hours ago treated with primary PCI to the proximal LAD with successful stent deployment and TIMI 3 flow. Since return from the catheter laboratory he has developed cardiogenic shock: MAP 55 mmHg despite noradrenaline at 0.4 microgram/kg/min plus adrenaline at 0.15 microgram/kg/min, lactate 5.8 mmol/L rising from 4.4, urine output 5 mL/h, and mottled peripheries. Bedside echocardiogram shows LV EF 20% with global anterior akinesis, no mechanical complication (no VSD, no papillary muscle rupture, no free wall rupture), no pericardial effusion. Right ventricular function is preserved. Coronary anatomy confirms complete revascularisation. He has been intubated 30 minutes ago and remains on high FiO2.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 112 (sinus tachycardia), blood pressure 92/38 with MAP 55, respiratory rate 22 (ventilated), SpO2 92% on FiO2 0.8, temperature 36.2 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: troponin 25000 ng/L (<30), lactate 5.8 mmol/L rising from 4.4 (<2), creatinine 168 micromol/L (60-110) rising from 90, mixed venous saturation 45%, echocardiogram LV EF 20%, global anterior akinesis, no mechanical complication, RV preserved, no effusion; ECG anterior Q waves with residual ST elevation
data_table.History: Anterior STEMI 6 hours ago, primary PCI proximal LAD with TIMI 3 flow, complete revascularisation, intubated 30 min ago

lead_in: According to the most contemporary Australian and international evidence, what is the most appropriate mechanical circulatory support decision?

options.text: Insert an intra-aortic balloon pump now and continue the current noradrenaline plus adrenaline vasoactive support
options.rationale: IABP-SHOCK II demonstrated no 30-day, 6-month or 12-month mortality benefit for IABP in post-STEMI cardiogenic shock, and current ESC guidelines downgraded IABP for this indication. It is not the correct escalation. (Source: ESC AMI/Cardiogenic Shock 2023)

options.text: Increase noradrenaline to 0.6 microgram/kg/min and add a vasopressin infusion at 0.03 units per minute together
options.rationale: Escalating vasoactive support in the presence of rising lactate, falling MAP despite maximal doses, and refractory shock will not restore end-organ perfusion; escalation of mechanical support is required. (Source: ESC AMI/Cardiogenic Shock 2023)

options.text: Commence a dobutamine infusion at 5 microgram/kg/min in addition to the current noradrenaline and adrenaline
options.rationale: Adding an ionodilator in refractory shock at high catecholamine burden with hypotension is unlikely to restore adequate cardiac output and may worsen hypotension; MCS is the required step at this level of refractory shock. (Source: ESC AMI/Cardiogenic Shock 2023)

options.text: Initiate emergency haemodialysis today for lactate clearance and continue current vasoactive support otherwise
options.rationale: Haemodialysis does not treat cardiogenic shock. Lactate clearance follows from restored perfusion; dialysis alone does not address the underlying pump failure and delays effective escalation. (Source: ESC AMI/Cardiogenic Shock 2023)

options.text: Initiate veno-arterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation as bridge to recovery with concurrent LV venting strategy
options.rationale: Post-STEMI cardiogenic shock refractory to maximal vasoactive and inotropic support with rising lactate, low mixed venous saturation, oliguria and severe LV dysfunction meets criteria for VA-ECMO bridge to recovery or decision. Australian tertiary centres provide this via ECMO retrieval services (Alfred, RPA, PA). VA-ECMO raises LV afterload and can precipitate pulmonary oedema through LV distension, so a concurrent LV venting strategy (Impella, IABP or atrial septostomy) is standard alongside VA-ECMO. Neither ECLS-SHOCK (2023) nor EURO-SHOCK confirmed mortality benefit in unselected populations, but selected refractory post-STEMI shock at high-volume centres remains an accepted indication. (Source: ESC AMI/Cardiogenic Shock 2023)

explanation.summary: Refractory post-STEMI cardiogenic shock (rising lactate, falling MAP despite maximal vasoactive plus inotropic therapy, low mixed venous saturation, oliguria) meets criteria for consideration of VA-ECMO bridge to recovery or decision. IABP alone has no evidence for benefit (IABP-SHOCK II) and has been downgraded. VA-ECMO raises LV afterload; concurrent venting via Impella, IABP or septostomy is standard to prevent pulmonary oedema. ECLS-SHOCK 2023 did not confirm benefit in unselected populations, but selected refractory cases at high-volume centres still receive VA-ECMO.
key_points: IABP in post-STEMI cardiogenic shock: no 30-day, 6-mo, 12-mo mortality benefit (IABP-SHOCK II); ESC downgraded
VA-ECMO for refractory shock: bridge to recovery or decision at high-volume centres despite neutral ECLS-SHOCK results
VA-ECMO raises LV afterload -> concurrent LV vent (Impella, IABP, septostomy) is standard
Australian centres accessed via state ECMO retrieval services
explanation.pearls: SCAI Shock stage E (refractory shock on high-dose vasoactives with rising lactate) has 30-day mortality >75% without MCS in some cohorts; early consultation with ECMO retrieval service improves candidate selection.
